q: We just closed a $400K deal. The AE is already off to the next one and the customer hasn't heard from anyone in two weeks. What should happen right now?
text:
## What's really going on

This is the first Inflection Point, the Purchase Moment. Right after buying, the customer is asking, "did I make the right decision?"[[1]] Two weeks of quiet works against you here, because silence after purchase is not neutral. It is the first loyalty blocker.[[2]]

The likely root cause is the handoff. In most organizations the handoff from sales to post-sale is treated as a transition, not a transfer of intelligence.[[3]] The book also explains why this keeps happening: Sales is closing the next deal. Finance is processing the contract. Customer Success is finishing a handoff somewhere else. Internally, a lot is happening. Externally, the customer hears nothing.[[4]]

## The play to run

Run the **Purchase & Welcome Play** now, and move straight into the **Kickoff Play** afterward. Purchase & Welcome exists to replace that silence with momentum, and to answer the question the customer is already asking: yes, you made the right decision, and here is what happens next.[[5]] It weaves together personalization, celebration, and expectation-setting.[[6]] You are recovering a missed window here rather than running the play on schedule. [[applied]]

## Your next 3 moves

1. **The AE completes the Internal Knowledge Transfer this week, before anything else goes out.** The IKT covers four questions: Why did they purchase? Who are they as a company, and who matters? What was sold, what was promised, and what was left out? What does success mean in their own words?[[7]] The answers should live in the CRM as a required field set — not in a sales rep's inbox.[[8]]

2. **The CSM sends personalized outreach as soon as the IKT is in hand.** The book describes this step as a welcome note or short video that reflects the customer's specific goals and creates confidence before kickoff.[[9]] Because the customer has already waited two weeks, the note should acknowledge the gap briefly and then move to what happens next. [[applied]] The book also suggests telling the customer who they bought from, since that story is one of the most effective tools against buyer's remorse[[10]].

3. **The CSM schedules the kickoff, and the CS leader secures the AE's attendance.** The scheduling request should clarify who should attend and why, what the customer should bring or prepare, and what to expect from the meeting.[[11]] On the seller's role, Tim writes, "I advocate for having the seller in the kickoff meeting." The reason is that the seller is the one person who can answer, on the spot, the questions that come out of the sales conversation[[12]]. The CS leader should also make sure the next closed deal triggers this sequence automatically, without anyone having to remember. [[applied]]

## What to hold off on

Don't let the urge to make up for lost time turn kickoff into a feature tour. The book is direct on this point: Kickoff is not product training. It is the first working conversation where two companies align around outcomes, roles, expectations, and the path to First Value.[[13]]

## How you'll know it's working

Watch for evidence that the customer is progressing, not for completed tasks. At the Purchase Moment, the evidence is that the post-sale team can state the reason for purchase, the customer confirms it, and any gap between what was sold and what can be delivered is surfaced early[[14]]. At kickoff, the customer restates the reason for purchase and the First Value target in their own words and commits to next steps with owners on their side[[15]].

A no-show at kickoff is a warning sign, because it means the welcome sequence did not create enough clarity or urgency to make the meeting feel important.[[16]]

On the pipeline side, this $400K renewal enters the Identify stage of the post-sale pipeline at purchase[[17]]. It stays in Identify until First Value[[18]], so getting to kickoff quickly is what starts its clock toward real evidence.

q: Sales promised the customer things during the deal that CS didn't know about. How do we stop finding out at kickoff?
text:
## What's really going on

This is a failure at the first Inflection Point, the Purchase Moment, which the Purchase & Welcome Play is designed to serve. The root cause is structural, not personal: in most organizations the handoff from sales to post-sale is treated as a transition, not a transfer of intelligence.[[1]] When that happens, Identify begins at a disadvantage because the team is forced to rediscover what the company already learned once.[[2]] The book also notes that this problem starts outside CS. If the use case was oversold or poorly qualified, Customer Success inherits a relationship that is already misaligned before it begins.[[3]]

## The play to run

Run the Purchase & Welcome Play, anchored on the Internal Knowledge Transfer (IKT). The IKT answers four questions that Sales must capture before the handoff is complete: Why did they purchase? Who are they as a company, and who matters? What was sold, what was promised, and what was left out? What does success mean in their own words?[[4]] The third question targets your exact problem. The IKT should live in the CRM as a required field set — not in a sales rep's inbox.[[5]]

Back it up in the Kickoff Play. The book recommends the kickoff should cover what the customer did not buy. If there is something they will need later and do not have, kickoff is the moment to say so.[[6]]

## Your next 3 moves

1. **CS leader, with the Sales leader:** Make the IKT a hard gate. A CRM configured to require IKT fields before a Closed-Won opportunity can progress to onboarding does not rely on the CSM remembering to ask for the handoff. The system enforces the play.[[7]]
2. **AE:** Attend every kickoff. Tim writes, "I advocate for having the seller in the kickoff meeting." The reason is that the seller is the one person who can answer, on the spot, the questions that come out of the sales conversation: what was discussed, what was promised, and what was meant.[[8]]
3. **CS leader:** Review IKT gaps weekly with Sales. Start with the five most recent deals this week. [[applied]] The book frames blank fields as not a data problem — it is a coaching conversation.[[9]]

## How you'll know it's working

These are team measures. Track IKT completion rate before CSM assignment, time from Closed-Won to first customer communication, and time from first communication to kickoff scheduled.[[10]] These metrics tell you whether the play is running consistently or only when someone remembers to run it.[[11]]

Over time, customers with complete kickoff data should be compared to customers without it.[[12]] In a shared pipeline review, Sales sees whether what was promised became evidence.[[13]] The qualitative signal is that kickoff stops surfacing surprises. Customers are no longer re-explaining the deal. Instead, they are invited to refine, correct, and deepen what your team already understands.[[14]]

q: Our kickoff meetings are just a slide tour and a project timeline. Customers leave without knowing what success looks like. How should a kickoff actually work?
text:
## What's really going on

This is the **First Meeting** Inflection Point, served by the **Kickoff Play**. The likely root cause is that your kickoff has become a transfer of information rather than an alignment conversation. The book describes this pattern: the customer hears a lot about the product before they hear enough about the path. They are shown what the system can do before the two companies have agreed on what the customer is trying to accomplish. The meeting becomes a transfer of information instead of a foundation for trust.[[1]] The book's operating principle is that kickoff is not product training. It is the first working conversation where two companies align around outcomes, roles, expectations, and the path to First Value.[[2]]

## The play to run

Run the canonical Kickoff Play. The meeting should follow a standard flow: introductions, the customer's journey and a review of what was purchased, the Five Questions, expectations, First Value, and next steps.[[3]]

The Five Questions directly fix your "no definition of success" gap:
1. What is the one thing we must get right to make this worth undertaking?[[4]]
2. How does your organization define success?[[5]]
3. What is our role in achieving that success?[[6]]
4. What aspects of the internal culture or external environment could put this effort at risk to fail?[[7]]
5. Assuming we mitigate that risk, what would exceed your wildest dreams?[[8]]

Each participant should have an opportunity to respond, and the most senior person in the room should answer last.[[9]] The kickoff team should then help translate that outcome into the first achievable win.[[10]]

## Your next 3 moves

1. **The CS leader** rebuilds the kickoff deck template around the standard flow. The book's guidance is to standardize the structure and customize the conversation.[[11]]
2. **The AE** completes the Internal Knowledge Transfer before handoff, answering Why did they purchase? Who are they as a company, and who matters? What was sold, what was promised, and what was left out? What does success mean in their own words?[[12]] The AE then attends the kickoff meeting. Tim writes, "I advocate for having the seller in the kickoff meeting."
3. **The CSM** captures the answers to the Five Questions and sends a follow-through email that should summarize decisions, action items, owners, due dates, materials, and the chosen First Value goal.[[13]] The Five Questions answers should not live only in a document. They should be captured in the CRM or customer platform.[[14]]

## What to hold off on

Don't replace the slide tour with heavier custom slides. The book warns that if the team believes every strong kickoff requires a heavily customized presentation, the play will become too slow and too dependent on individual effort.[[15]]

## How you'll know it's working

**Team measures:** At a minimum, the team should know how quickly kickoff occurs after purchase, whether the right people attended, whether the Five Questions were captured, whether First Value was defined, whether follow-through was sent within the expected timeframe, and whether the next meeting was scheduled before momentum faded.[[16]]

**Evidence across accounts:** watch for kickoffs where the customer restates the reason for purchase and the First Value target in their own words and commits to next steps with owners on their side[[17]].

Over time, customers with a clearly defined First Value goal should be compared to customers who entered onboarding without one.[[18]]

q: We're a startup with 30 customers and no CS tooling at all. Is this method too heavy for us?
text:
## What's really going on

This is a sequencing question, not a sizing question. The book says the most common failure mode is enthusiasm without sequence — trying to install all twenty-two chapters at once, stalling in the complexity, and concluding the system does not work.[[1]] Your size helps you. At small scale, this is manageable. A strong team can compensate for the lack of structure.[[2]] The risk comes later: without a unifying structure, adding people does not reduce variability—it multiplies it.[[3]] At 30 customers you can lay down structure cheaply, before that strain arrives. [[applied]]

Having no tooling does not block you. The pipeline runs on evidence the team already captures in its daily work, not on usage telemetry, it works even in organizations convinced they don't have the data for it.[[4]] The Data Spine is not a product category or a specific platform.[[5]]

## The play to run

Start by defining progression, then run one play. Defining progression costs nothing but thinking, which is exactly why data-poor organizations can start here. The system works before the data does.[[6]]

For the play, the book says to run one play well. Not eight. One.[[7]] The Alignment Meeting is the strongest anchor for an established book of business; Kickoff is the right anchor when most customers are new.[[8]] If most of your 30 customers signed recently, choose the Kickoff Play. If they are mostly past onboarding, choose the Alignment Meeting Play. [[applied]]

## Your next 3 moves

1. **CS leader (or founder):** Write down what should change for customers at each inflection point and what First Value means for your top segment. Then write the pipeline stages and the exit criteria revenue opportunities must meet.[[9]] At your size, one working session should be enough to draft this. [[applied]]
2. **CS leader:** Pick the system of record, define the fields that describe progression, and retire the local copies. If it is not in the system, it does not exist.[[10]] If you already use a CRM for sales, that can serve as the system of record. [[applied]]
3. **CSM:** Build the chosen play's assets (brief, agenda, follow-through template[[11]]), then run the play across the book, not just with friendly accounts.[[12]]

## What to hold off on

Don't start with health scoring or automation. The book says to turn on health scoring once the system is producing enough evidence about progression, value, and relationships to interpret[[13]], and to never automate an undefined motion — that only accelerates inconsistency.[[14]]

## How you'll know it's working

These are **team measures**, taken from the book's 90-day path:

- You inspect weekly: whether the play ran, whether the expected change occurred, and what the evidence means for each opportunity and next action.[[15]]
- If you run Kickoff, track how quickly kickoff occurs after purchase, whether the right people attended, whether the Five Questions were captured, whether First Value was defined, whether follow-through was sent within the expected timeframe, and whether the next meeting was scheduled before momentum faded.[[16]]
- At day 90, the win is not a retention number. It is a leadership conversation that starts with evidence: here is the motion we designed, here is how consistently it ran, and here is what the evidence tells us to do next.[[17]]

If you'd like help adapting this sequence to your specific mix of customers, an intro call with Tim is a good next step. [[applied]]

q: One of our accounts is at risk.
text:
Before recommending a play, the CXology Desk needs two facts, because each one points to a different play:

1. **Where is the account in its lifecycle?** Is it a first-term customer that hasn't yet reached First Value, or is it past First Value, and how many months remain until renewal?
2. **What made you flag it as at risk?** For example, did a champion or executive sponsor leave, did usage drop, did a First Value date pass, did priorities or budget change, or did the customer go quiet?

These answers matter because the book handles these situations differently. In the first term, the renewal stays in Identify until the customer reaches First Value, because a customer who has not yet experienced a meaningful result from what they bought is a renewal at real risk.[[1]] A departed contact calls for a different response: when the advocate leaves or loses influence, the opportunity moves back to Align until a new carrier is in place.[[2]] The book's Key Contact Change play exists for that case. A usage drop is a third situation. A drop in usage, a red health score, or a CSM's concern does not move a stage back on its own. These signals don't advance a stage, so they don't reverse one either. They should trigger a check of whether the evidence still holds.[[3]]

q: What price should we charge for our product?
text:
The book doesn't cover how to set the price of your product. It has no pricing frameworks, price points, or packaging guidance, so the CXology Desk can't recommend a number or a method.

Here are the three closest ideas the documents do cover:

1. **Pricing is one of three systems that meet at renewal.** The book describes renewal as the place where three systems meet. The first is the value system: what the customer hoped to accomplish, what progress has been made, and what still matters.[[1]] The second is the customer's buying system: how budgets are set, who approves, how procurement and legal work, and whether a new executive or a vendor-consolidation mandate has changed the rules.[[2]] The third is your commercial system: terms, pricing, timing, expansion paths, and the handoff between CS and Sales.[[3]] A strong play brings these into alignment before they collide.[[4]] The book treats pricing as something to align with value and with how the customer buys. It does not tell you how to set it.

2. **A cautionary tale about when billing starts.** The First Value chapter tells the story of a company where saying yes was easy, partly because the company did not charge anything until after Go Live.[[5]] Then onboarding dragged on, customers became overwhelmed, and many gave up before they ever went live.[[6]] Because billing started at Go Live, every hour spent finding, selling, and onboarding those customers became a loss, and it hurt morale as much as revenue.[[7]] The book's lesson is that the product was never the problem. The customers simply never reached a first win.[[8]]

3. **Your post-sale experience has a cost your price must cover.** The book frames capacity planning as the financial expression of your post-sale strategy.[[9]] It notes that every service moment is a customer experience decision, but it is also a resource decision.[[10]] Knowing the designed effort behind each segment's experience can inform pricing conversations, but the book stops short of connecting the two. [[applied]]

**Suggested next step:** pricing strategy is outside what the book addresses. An intro call with Tim is the best way to explore whether and how CXology can help with your question.

q: Is Gainsight or Vitally the better CS platform?
text:
The book does not compare Gainsight, Vitally, or any other CS platform, so the CXology Desk can't recommend one over the other. Gainsight appears only as the source of an industry benchmark on CSM ratios, not as a product evaluation.

Here are the three closest ideas the book does cover:

1. **The system comes before the tool.** The book treats the Data Spine as architecture, not software. It is not a product category or a specific platform.[[1]] It is a design principle: every customer-facing system — CRM, CS platform, support desk, professional services automation, product telemetry — is integrated such that the customer record in the designated source of truth reflects reality at all times.[[2]]

2. **Sequence matters more than selection.** The book's build order starts with defining progression, then building the data spine. That means you pick the system of record, define the fields that describe progression, and retire the local copies.[[3]] On technology choices in general, the book says deploying AI well requires treating it as an infrastructure decision, not a tool selection.[[4]] It adds that the questions that matter most are not which AI products to use (those will continue to change) but how AI is embedded into the plays, the data, and the operating rhythm of the team.[[5]]

3. **A platform only helps if it can enforce the plays.** The book favors structured data entry: dropdown menus, standardized field options, required fields with validation rules, and structured templates force consistency at the point of entry.[[6]] It also gives examples of the system enforcing a stage, such as a renewal that cannot move to Intent without a recorded commitment and approval path, an expansion opportunity that cannot enter Advocate without a recorded advocate.[[7]]

A practical next step is to write down your pipeline stages, exit criteria, and First Value definition first, and then test each platform on whether it can hold that record and enforce those rules. [[applied]] For a direct recommendation on tooling, an intro call with Tim is the best route.

q: What NPS score is considered good for B2B SaaS?
text:
## The short answer

The book does not give an NPS benchmark or say what score counts as "good" for B2B SaaS. The CXology Desk can't give you a number from these materials. Here are the three closest ideas the book does cover.

## The closest ideas the book offers

**1. NPS belongs in a health model, but it shouldn't carry the score.** The book places NPS among the traditional criteria. It says usage, NPS, support case volume, renewal timing, purchase history, and CSM judgment can all provide context. But they should not carry the whole score.[[1]] The reason it gives is that traditional indicators are often easier to collect than they are to interpret.[[2]]

**2. Other signals may matter more than NPS.** When weighting a health score, the book notes that not every signal has equal predictive power.[[3]] One example it gives is that lack of executive visibility may matter more than a neutral NPS response.[[4]] It recommends that the weight reflect the degree to which each criterion helps predict future behavior and the degree to which the company can act on it.[[5]]

**3. Sentiment signals tend to arrive late.** The book groups sentiment with usage, adoption, and engagement as valuable signals, and nothing here argues for ignoring them. The point is timing and interpretation. Many metrics commonly called leading indicators appear after earlier customer progression has already succeeded or failed.[[6]] Instead of asking whether a customer is red, the book suggests a different question: "Given everything we can see, is this customer progressing toward the outcomes they bought for, and are they able to sustain them?"[[7]]

## A suggested next step

The book's approach would point you away from an external NPS target. Instead, it would have you decide how much weight NPS deserves in your own health model. To do that, the book recommends looking at your healthiest customers. Look at the customers you would happily clone.[[8]] [[applied]]

If you need help setting an NPS target or interpreting your scores, consider booking an intro call with Tim.

q: RevOps question: when a renewal forecast doesn't line up with the account notes, customer health, or stated next steps, where do we draw the line between reporting the forecast and influencing the strategy? How does RevOps get enough context to say more than "the data says X" without becoming Sales Management?
text:
## What's really going on
The forecast and the account notes disagree because the renewal is being forecast on opinion, not evidence. The book's example of that kind of judgment is a stage call like "I think they're green. They'll renew."[[1]] The underlying gap isn't data: more customer data doesn't automatically create that visibility.[[2]] That's an operating-system problem.[[3]]
**Book gap:** the book doesn't define where RevOps ends and Sales Management begins. It does define a third option: make the evidence standard the thing everyone debates.[[applied]]
## The play to run
Run **post-sale pipeline reviews** on a set cadence: inspect what moved forward, what moved back, what stalled, and why, the same way sales reviews its pipeline.[[4]] The goal isn't to remove judgment from the forecast. It's to give judgment a common structure and an evidence trail.[[5]]
## Your next 3 moves
1. **RevOps: require every renewal to carry the same fields.** indicated value, stage, probability, expected close date, evidence, next action, and owner. A renewal missing evidence for its stage is a data gap, squarely in RevOps's lane, not a strategy opinion.[[applied]]
2. **RevOps, in the forecast review: ask the evidence question, not the strategy question.** When someone disagrees about a stage, the conversation moves from opinion to evidence: what would prove the next exit criterion, and who is going to get it.[[6]] The pipeline moves on evidence, not on the team's sense that advocacy exists,[[7]] and not on forecast optimism or friendly signals.[[8]]
3. **RevOps with the CS leader: get context from CS, not by becoming Sales.** After Closed Won, much of the evidence is customer progression, which is different from activity, which only tells us what the team did.[[9]] CS is closest to that evidence, so partner with CS for it.[[applied]] Keep health and commitment separate: a customer can be healthy without having committed to renew.[[10]]
## How you'll know it's working
Stage disagreements end with a named exit criterion and an owner instead of a debate.[[6]] RevOps's voice in forecast reviews carries weight because it rests on evidence, not tenure: judgment still matters, it just works inside a shared structure.[[11]]

q: RevOps question: when a renewal forecast doesn't line up with the account notes, customer health, or stated next steps, where do we draw the line between reporting the forecast and influencing the strategy? How does RevOps get enough context to say more than "the data says X" without becoming Sales Management?
text:
## What's really going on

This is a management-discipline problem in the Post-Sale Pipeline. It is not a judgment call about who gets to have an opinion. When the forecast, the notes, and the health score disagree, the usual cause is that the stage isn't tied to evidence. In the book's model, the stage is not determined by what your team did. It is determined by what you can prove about the opportunity.[[1]] Health and stage also answer different questions. Health describes the state of the customer. The pipeline shows where each revenue opportunity stands and what evidence supports that position.[[2]]

The line you're looking for is already drawn in the book's model. None of this requires RevOps to take ownership of customer relationships or Customer Success to become a sales organization. It requires a shared operating model. Customer-facing teams own the work and the relationships. Revenue leadership establishes expectations for visibility, evidence, and forecast discipline.[[3]]

## The play to run

Run an evidence-based pipeline review as a whole-company operating review, not as a reporting meeting. In that review, Customer Success sees which opportunities rest on thin or stale evidence. RevOps sees whether the probabilities and amounts are holding up.[[4]] The aim is action: they decide what work happens next. A review that only explains the number has not done its job.[[5]]

This is how RevOps says more than "the data says X" without managing the CSM. RevOps asks for the evidence and the next action. CS decides which play to run. When people disagree, the conversation moves from opinion to evidence: what would prove the next exit criterion, and who is going to get it.[[6]]

## Your next 3 moves

1. **RevOps and the CS leader** standardize the record so context lives in the system rather than in the CSM's head. Every opportunity should carry indicated value, stage, probability, expected close date and its source, evidence and the date it was last verified, next action, and owner. First-term renewals also carry an expected First Value date until First Value is reached.[[7]] The stage probabilities (20/40/60/90/100%) are CXology planning assumptions, not measured benchmarks.
2. **RevOps** freezes the forecast at the start of each quarter. At quarter end, RevOps sorts each difference by its source: outcome, amount, timing, or new opportunities.[[8]] That breakdown gives you a factual basis for raising strategy questions. [[applied]]
3. **The CS leader** chairs the weekly review, with RevOps preparing the list. The questions are: What moved? What moved back? What's stuck? What's overdue? What's stale?[[9]][[10]][[11]][[12]][[13]] For each mismatch, the **CSM** owns the next action, and RevOps tracks whether it happened. [[applied]]

## What to hold off on

Don't let RevOps re-stage deals or cut amounts based on dashboards. A drop in usage, a red health score, or a CSM's concern doesn't move an opportunity back on its own. These don't advance a stage, so they don't reverse one either. They should trigger a check of whether the evidence still holds.[[14]] The same applies to amounts: a usage drop, a health score, or an internal concern doesn't change the amount on its own. It triggers investigation.[[15]]

## How you'll know it's working

These are team measures:
- Forecast accuracy, defined as how closely the quarter's starting forecast matched the decisions that actually became final, and whether misses came from timing, outcomes, amounts, or evidence that did not hold.[[16]]
- Fewer opportunities with blank evidence, missing next actions, or stale verification dates. [[applied]]
- Reviews where teams report what the system saw, not what the team felt.[[17]]
